newsitem.title: FRANCE: Doctors shutter offices in protest of reform plans.
newsitem.headline: Doctors shutter offices in protest of reform plans.

text.p: Several thousand specialist doctors across France closed their offices on Thursday to protest government plans to slash health care spending as part of its deficit-fighting efforts, union officials said.
"The number of offices closed today is slightly over 60 percent," Dr Christian Le Goff, a member of the CSMF doctors union told Reuters.

The protest was partly spurred by a threat earlier this week by the national health assurance fund (CNAM) to invalidate the doctors' agreement on working conditions if the unions did not sign an accord on reform by November 15.
Three unions are in negotiations on reforms with the CNAM, but some, led by the hard-line SML doctors group, refuses to even talk to the government.
"At a time of crisis, we cannot negotiate, especially with a knife to our throat," said Dr Jean-Francois Giorla, vice president of the SML.

"The pre-condition to negotiations is the pure and simple lifting of the sanctions which hit doctors, expecially those financial sanctions that are retroactive for 1995 which are applied indiscriminately," Giorla added.
The protest was the second in two weeks by the doctors. Last week, some 80 percent of the doctors in the Alpes-Maritime region heeded a union call to shut their offices, unions said.

Many French doctors are particularly unhappy about a plan to force them to meet government health spending targets. Under the plan, if doctors overspend, they would have to return some of their revenues from patients' fees to the government.
Doctors unions opposing the change have said they believe this could lead to rationing of care.
For 1996, the government has set a target for growth in non-hospital spending of 2.1 percent.

But France's largest doctors' union, MG France is in favour of the reform plan, which would also impose more enforceable medical standards, introduce mandatory health cards and could eventually mandate visits to generalists before a specialist call would be permitted.
The plan also provides for computerising doctors offices and the introduction of generic drugs.
